title: Seeing Should Probably Not Be Believing: The Role of Deceptive Support in COVID-19 Misinformation on Twitter
screen_reason: Primarily an NLP detection-pipeline paper (check-worthiness classification + support verification), which is an EXCLUDE ground on its own. But it also reports a descriptive share of items judged misleading with an explicit denominator: 55 of approximately 5,000 test tweets (1%) carry 'deceptive support', i.e. a check-worthy claim not supported by the news article the tweet cites, judged by three human annotators (Fleiss kappa = 0.756). That satisfies CONTENT. Included with borderline=true on both rows; see missed_or_uncertain for the argument for EXCLUDE.

estimates.measure_type: % of check-worthy COVID-19 tweets citing a major news article whose cited article does not actually support the claim (deceptive support / misleading)
estimates.denominator: approximately 5,000 English-language COVID-19 tweets in the held-out test set (single-sentence, check-worthy, each linking to one of 27 top English-language news domains), drawn from 46,117 filtered tweets
estimates.definition: A tweet makes a check-worthy factual claim and cites a news article, but no information in that article supports the claim; labelled 'unsupported' by at least two of three independent annotators who read the whole article.
estimates.misinfo_def: Posts that cite a news article but present claims unsupported by the source are candidates for misinformation.
estimates.source_quote: Of the 200 manual annotations discussed above, 55 are labeled as deceptive (i.e., 27.5%). This, however, is sampled from the test of approximately 5,000 Tweets. Thus, our test data show that at least 55 of 5,000 Tweets (i.e., 1%) contain deceptive hyperlinks.
estimates.page_loc: Section 5.2.1 Sample Annotation, p. 9:14; also abstract and Section 7 Conclusion
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three annotators independently judged each tweet-article pair as supported or unsupported after reading the full article; majority label used; Fleiss kappa = 0.756 (substantial agreement). Selection of the 258 pairs that were annotated was made by the classifiers (weakly false negatives), so the 1% is an explicit LOWER BOUND, not an unbiased prevalence: tweets the model never flagged were never checked by a human.
estimates.moderator_quote: Tweets with no external link to one of these domains are removed from our study.
estimates.notes: The paper says 'at least' 1%: the numerator counts only deceptive tweets that the model surfaced as candidates, so the true share of misleading tweets in the denominator is unknown and higher. Denominator is doubly filtered (52 COVID keywords, then a link to one of 27 Alexa top-50 English news domains, then classifier-judged check-worthy, then single-sentence only), hence denom_selection=curated. Country is not stated; only English-language tweets were kept, and the news domains are mostly US/UK, but no country breakdown is given, so coded Global.

estimates.measure_type: % of model-flagged candidate tweet-article pairs that human annotators judged deceptive (unsupported by the cited article)
estimates.value_raw: Of the 200 manual annotations discussed above, 55 are labeled as deceptive (i.e., 27.5%)
estimates.denominator: 200 annotated tweet-headline pairs (of 258 flagged by the classifiers as weakly false negatives, after discarding 51 judged not check-worthy and 7 with annotator disagreement)
estimates.definition: Pair labelled 'unsupported' by at least two of three annotators after reading the full cited article.
estimates.misinfo_def: Posts that cite a news article but present claims unsupported by the source are candidates for misinformation.
estimates.source_quote: Of the 258 pairs, 51 were labeled as not check-worthy by at least two annotators. We discard these from the evaluation of the second step. Further, there were disagreements on 7 other Tweets, which we discard as well. Of the remaining 200 pairs, 55 were labeled as unsupported by at least two annotators.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same three-annotator procedure, Fleiss kappa = 0.756. The denominator here is the set of pairs the classifiers had already flagged as suspicious, so this figure is the pipeline's positive predictive value, not a prevalence.
estimates.moderator_quote: Thus, we collect these weakly false negative Tweet, headline pairs and feed them to the second step where the classifiers investigate entire articles.
estimates.notes: Flagged within_misinfo_content=true because the denominator was pre-selected by the model to be misinformation-suspicious; the 27.5% therefore cannot enter a prevalence pool. Kept because the abstract and conclusion both report it as a headline number, so an adjudicator should see it and decide. QUOTE NOTE (validator repair, this session): source_quote carries quote_verbatim=false because the PDF text renders 'two annotators' as the run-together string 'twoannotators'; the quote restores the space and is otherwise word-for-word.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Screening judgement an adjudicator should check: this is a detection/classifier paper, an explicit EXCLUDE ground, and both usable numbers are by-products of the classification pipeline rather than a designed prevalence measurement. A defensible alternative call is EXCLUDE (classifier/modelling work). I included it because the instructions say a study whose aim is something else is still included if a descriptive share with a denominator is reported, and 'at least 1% ... contain deceptive hyperlinks' is exactly that. 2) NOT extracted: the abstract's '43.4% of the Tweets are not factual and hence not worth checking'. That is a share of non-check-worthy (subjective/opinion) posts, not a share of false or misleading content, so it is not a misinformation prevalence estimate. The figure also does not reconcile with any denominator given in the body (46,117 -> 39,458 fed forward), so I could not tie it to a stated n. 3) NOT extracted: 'approximately 54% of all the Tweets provided as input to our second task' are near-verbatim reproductions of the news headline (a faithfulness statistic, not falsity). 4) NOT extracted: '24-33% (varying between the various models) of the weakly false negative samples are, indeed, unsupported' (Section 5.3) and the per-model TN columns of Table 6 - these are model-performance ranges over classifier-flagged subsets, not prevalence. 5) NOT extracted: the intro's citation of Kouzy et al. ('nearly 25% of them included misinformation') - a figure the paper cites from elsewhere, barred by R8. 6) Country: the paper never states one; only English-language tweets and mostly US news domains, coded Global rather than United States.

rob.design: Secondary analysis of the Banda et al. open COVID-19 Twitter archive (383M tweets, Jan-Jun 2020); a 46.86M-tweet March-May 2020 subset was filtered to English, non-retweet, containing at least one of 52 COVID keywords, and linking to one of 27 top Alexa English-language news domains, yielding 46,117 tweets and 23,841 unique news articles. An XLNet-Base check-worthiness classifier (tuned on ClaimBuster + a CLEF COVID tweet set, evaluated on 100 hand-labelled tweets, Fleiss kappa = 0.822) passed 39,458 tweets forward; a single-sentence filter left 29,392 (11,800 train / 12,335 validation / 5,257 test). Veracity ground truth comes only from a 258-pair annotation of classifier-flagged candidates by three annotators (Fleiss kappa = 0.756), 200 retained. No random sample of the corpus was ever hand-coded, so the reported prevalence is a lower bound of unknown tightness. No response rate applies (platform data). Country and demographics of posters unknown.
